items.body: MoE, the vocals, guitar and bass duo of Guro Moe and Håvard Skaset, is one of the most interesting rock acts around today, merging aggression and a punk attitude and with a love for improvised and experimental music. On this release they're joined by frequent collaborator Ikuro Takahashi on drums and alto saxophonist powerhouse Signe Emmeluth. While collaboration and experimentation are to be expected with this band this record is notable for mainly two reasons: it was recorded live in concert (which came as a surprise to me because their chemistry is so great that I'd assumed a lot of their records were recorded live) and it's the first MoE album in which frontwoman and backbone of the band Guro Moe trades her trusty electric bass for a double bass. While each of the six untitled tracks has its own identity, the album is a full gig recording with the dynamics of a concert as a consequence. After a short minute of mood setting and acclimatization the four musicians get straight to business with pummeling, fluid drumming, furious guitar bashing and driving bass setting the stage for Emmeluth to shine on her sax. This no holds barred first track immediately shows just how tight this band is and will be throughout the album, the especially fantastic interplay between the sax and the guitar being a highlight. The second track brings the energy down a bit and rests on Moe's signature bass playing, simultaneously gluing the band together and laying down a delightfully off-kilter groove. Takahashi and Skaset take a step back, the former focusing mainly on the cymbals and the latter turning his guitar into something that resembles a synth pad, leaving the bass and sax to their polyrithmic dance. Track four, the midpoint of the concert, introduces hints of psychedelia, with its effects-heavy guitar and a saxophone that at times sounds like a half-remembered dream, but the music and the mood are in constant evolution and the underwater feeling is soon spirited away by a massive bowed bass riff and a desperate shriek. In the latter half of the album the music takes on a mysterious quality and something else takes center stage: Moe's fantastic vocal performance. While the vocals and lyrics are present throughout the record (MoE is a rock band at their core at the end of the day) it feels like at a certain point all four musicians collectively decide to give priority to the vocal performance for a while. And what a performance it is! Full of passion, melody and angst, ranging from hissing whispers to operatic highs, often in conversation and sync with Emmeluth's altissimo notes, it's endlessly engaging and captivating Takahashi and Skaset then take on a more active role, guiding the band towards a final crescendo of distortion, blister-inducing bass playing and squealing sax overtones. For the second time on the record the band proves to be just as capable at bringing the energy down as building it up, something arguably harder to do convincingly, and they close the concert out with a slithering bowed bassline enveloped by Moe's soaring vocals. All four musicians are extremely talented and have a very assertive voice. The challenge for the band then becomes creating music that's balanced and doesn't particularily revolve around any one musician and I think they pass this challenge with flying colors. The players know exactly what and when to play, when to be active and when to play support in order to serve the music first and foremost. Emmeluth in particular is fantastic at exchanging ideas with the others, always picking the right notes to embellish a guitar chord or supporting a vocal melody,. There are no flashy solos or traditional jazz or even rock forms, just collective creation of a kind of music that revolves around attitude and emotion. It's an elating, moving and lively album, beautifully recorded and presented. I hope to hear this lineup together again soon. Released on digitally and on CD by Conrad Sound . items.body:
KATSEYE are going WILD! The global girl group have released their third EP via HYBE x Geffen Records. Arriving on 14 August, the five-track project marks a new chapter for KATSEYE, capturing the growth and transformation they have experienced over the past two years.

The EP follows 2025's BEAUTIFUL CHAOS, which debuted in the top five of the Billboard 200 and earned the group a GRAMMY nomination. WILD features previously released singles 'PINKY UP' and 'Animal', alongside new tracks 'Hootie Frutti', 'Bel Air', and 'That Way'.

Coinciding with the EP's arrival is the official music video for 'Hootie Frutti'. Driven by Brazilian phonk-inspired percussion and maximalist pop production, the track sees KATSEYE leaning into a fiercer, more playful side. Its music video takes the group to a vibrant underground Brazilian party on the verge of wrapping up — until KATSEYE arrive and bring the energy back to life. Alfred Marroquin directed the visual, with production by Somesuch.

Elsewhere on WILD, 'Bel Air' explores the bittersweet feeling of outgrowing something once loved, while closing track 'That Way' turns its attention to power dynamics and desire. The project also includes 'Animal', a flirtatious pop anthem co-written by Ed Sheeran, and 'PINKY UP', which made its live debut at Coachella.

Physical editions available through Target and international retailers also include the bonus track 'Unloveu', written and produced by KATSEYE member Lara Raj alongside Amy Allen and Ross Golan.

The release arrives as KATSEYE gear up for their sold-out THE WILDWORLD TOUR, which begins at Dublin's 3Arena on 1 September. The global arena tour sold out in under 48 hours and includes two-night stops at The O2 in London, UBS Arena in Belmont Park, Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, and Palacio de los Deportes in Mexico City.

KATSEYE have also brought the WILD era to the big screen with KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS. Directed by Nadia Hallgren, the film features never-before-seen footage, EYEKONS fan videos, and interviews exploring the relationship between the group and their global fandom. Following its 4 August premiere at The Grove in Los Angeles, the film began a limited engagement across 1,700 cinemas in more than 60 countries. The movie is now showing at Shaw Theatres in Singapore.

Orchard Road is getting a dose of F1 action and live music this August. BABYMONSTER are teaming up with adidas and the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS Formula 1 Team for adidas Orchard Ignition, happening on 29 and 30 August. The two-day takeover will bring motorsport, music, and culture to the heart of Singapore ahead of Grand Prix™ Season Singapore (GPSS).

Expected to draw more than 30,000 fans, the event will feature a Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team Guided Garage Tour, a Live Race Car Demo and Hot Laps along Orchard Road, as well as a Fan Festival featuring BABYMONSTER, Benjamin Kheng, Iman Fandi, and DJ KIARA.

BABYMONSTER are hitting the streets of Orchard Road

On 30 August, Orchard Road will be transformed into an approximately 600-metre temporary street track for Singapore's first F1 Live Race Car Demo in over a decade.

Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team reserve driver Fred Vesti will take the wheel for a series of high-speed demonstrations along the stretch between Paragon and TANGS at Tang Plaza.

BABYMONSTER will officially flag off the showcase before joining the action themselves for Hot Laps in a Mercedes-AMG car sporting a Singapore-exclusive livery. Fans will also be able to catch live in-car broadcast feeds from the experience.

The Live Race Car Demo and Hot Laps are free and open to the public, with dedicated viewing areas along Orchard Road. Selected fans will also be able to win access to VIP Viewing Decks.

The day's schedule is as follows:

3 PM – 3:10 PM: Live Race Car Demo Session 1

3:10 PM – 3:20 PM: Hot Laps with BABYMONSTER

3:30 PM – 3:35 PM: Live Race Car Demo Session 2

3:45 PM – 3:50 PM: Live Race Car Demo Session 3

Timings are subject to change.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by adidas Motorsport (@adidasmotorsport)

BABYMONSTER, Benjamin Kheng, Iman Fandi, and DJ KIARA head to Design Orchard

Once the engines quiet down, the festivities will continue at Design Orchard's rooftop amphitheatre for the Fan Festival.

BABYMONSTER will make a special appearance for a fan engagement session from 6 PM to 6:35 PM, which will be open exclusively to ticketed winners.

From 6:35 PM, Benjamin Kheng and Iman Fandi will take the stage for live performances, before DJ KIARA closes out the evening with a high-energy set. The performances are free and open to the public, subject to controlled entry and available capacity.

Fan Festival details:

Date: 30 August

Time: 4 PM – 10 PM

Venue: Design Orchard, 250 Orchard Road, Singapore 238905

BABYMONSTER fan engagement: 6 PM – 6:35 PM, ticketed winners only

Live performances: 6:35 PM – 9 PM, free and open to the public subject to capacity

Go behind the scenes with Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by adidas Singapore (@adidassg)

A day before the Orchard Road action, fans can get a closer look at the world of Formula 1 at the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team Garage pop-up outside adidas Brand Centre Orchard on 29 August.

Open to the public from 10 AM to 8:45 PM, the pop-up takes inspiration from track-side hospitality and team garage environments. Selected fans will be able to join 15-minute Guided Garage Tour sessions and meet Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team technicians as they prepare the car for its Orchard Road demonstration.

How to win access to adidas Orchard Ignition

From 14 to 25 August, fans can enter a series of promotions across adidas stores, adidas.com.sg, the adidas App, retail partners, and participating Orchard Road outlets for a chance to score access to the Guided Garage Tour, VIP Viewing Decks, and BABYMONSTER fan engagement at the Fan Festival.

Among the promotions, shoppers who spend SGD 250 — including at least one motorsport item — and exchange 500 adiClub points via the adidas App can enter for a chance to win an Ultimate Motorsport Experience for two, comprising access to all three activities. adiClub members can also exchange 500 points for a chance to win a pair of tickets to the Fan Festival featuring BABYMONSTER.

From 27 August to 17 September, fans who spend SGD 180, including at least one selected motorsport item, at participating adidas stores and online can also receive an exclusive BABYMONSTER bag charm or shoe charm, while stocks last.

adidas Orchard Ignition is supported by the Singapore Tourism Board and forms part of Grand Prix™ Season Singapore.

For the full promotion mechanics and latest event updates, fans can check adidas Singapore's Instagram and Facebook pages.

items.body:
BTS' RM and j-hope are facing backlash from fans after attending Chris Brown and Usher's The R&B Tour on 12 August in Toronto, sharing videos from the concert, and later appearing in backstage photos with Brown.

The two BTS members were at Rogers Stadium for the second of Brown and Usher's two Toronto shows. While their attendance quickly caught fans' attention, much of the criticism that followed centred on their visible support for the concert and subsequent interaction with Brown.

j-hope shared several moments from the night through his personal Instagram account, including footage of Usher performing 'Yeah!' and Brown onstage. He also posted a selfie video of himself and RM dancing along to Brown's 'Look At Me Now'.

Brown later shared a photograph of himself posing backstage with RM and j-hope. Usher also posted images of the three together, including shots of them laughing, shaking hands, and walking backstage.

The posts have since fuelled criticism across parts of the BTS fandom, with fans questioning RM and j-hope's decision to publicly associate themselves with Brown given his history of violence and legal controversies.

Omfg it just keeps getting worse. I might be too woke but this is too much pic.twitter.com/rrjTiUyb94

— mari - saw bts!!! (@urfavvcrazygirl) August 13, 2026

Fans criticise RM and j-hope over public association with Brown

Much of the backlash has focused not simply on RM and j-hope being present at the concert, but on the videos and photographs that followed.

Fans on a BTS-focused subreddit criticised the pair's judgement, with one describing the appearance as "thoughtless male privilege behaviour". Another said that "their judgment is not always the best". Other fans voiced their disappointment on X.

Other fans questioned why members of a group with a predominantly female fanbase would attend Brown's concert. Reports cited one post that read: "when u have a female dominated fanbase I think the least u can do is to not attend a famously known abuser's concert man idk".

Another fan connected the controversy to other recent discussions surrounding BTS, writing: "AI ads and chris brown support… are they trying to remind us that they're men and we should be disappointed in them or what".

The latter referred to separate criticism surrounding BTS' collaboration with Google Gemini, which had led some fans to use the hashtag #ARMYsAgainstAI.

Chris Brown's history is central to the backlash

The criticism surrounding RM and j-hope's appearance comes against the backdrop of Brown's long and widely documented legal history.

In 2009, Brown pleaded guilty to felony assault against his then-girlfriend Rihanna. He later served time in jail in 2014 for violating his probation. Brown has subsequently faced multiple allegations of sexual assault and violent behaviour in separate incidents. More recently, Brown pleaded guilty on 24 July to affray in connection with a 2023 altercation outside a London nightclub. His sentencing is scheduled for October.

Brown's presence in Toronto itself had also prompted questions because he had previously been denied entry to Canada. In February 2015, he cancelled concerts in Toronto and Montreal after being turned away at the Canadian border. His representative said at the time that Brown had been denied entry because of "immigration issues".

Speaking to The Toronto Star, immigration lawyers explained that people who may be inadmissible to Canada because of a criminal record can apply for temporary permission to enter the country.

Toronto immigration lawyer Evan Green said authorities may assess the risks of admitting an individual against the reasons for their visit. Montreal-based immigration lawyer Marisa Feil added that there is no separate immigration exemption for celebrities, although major performers can potentially demonstrate a significant reason for temporary entry because of the economic commitments tied to large-scale concerts.

Brown and Usher's Toronto shows were already courting controversy

RM and j-hope's appearance was not the only element of The R&B Tour attracting attention.

One of the tour's recurring segments sees Brown and Usher bring fans onstage during 'Can U Handle It?' for a sexually charged serenade.

At an earlier Nashville show, footage circulated of a fan appearing uncomfortable as Usher performed the routine. According to reports, the singer noticed her reaction and motioned for her to be taken offstage.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by USA TODAY Entertainment (@usatodayentertainment)

The segment generated further discussion during the first Toronto show after video circulated of Brown performing an explicit routine with a woman brought onstage.

That wider controversy has added another layer to the discussion surrounding RM and j-hope's presence at the concert, particularly as fans continued debating the pair's decision to post footage from the night and meet Brown backstage.

The appearance comes days before BTS' own Rogers Stadium shows

The timing has also drawn attention because BTS are set to perform at the same Toronto venue shortly afterwards. The group are scheduled to bring their ARIRANG world tour to Rogers Stadium for 22 and 23 August, as part of their ongoing North American run.

Neither RM nor j-hope has publicly addressed the backlash surrounding their attendance, social media posts, or backstage meeting with Brown at the time of writing.

items.body: This, unfortunately, digital only release is a treat, a future hidden gem, probably, for all those interested in the free thinking ethos of improvisation. Jack Wright is on the saxophones (alto and soprano, I believe) and Bennett on the drums and some other percussive objects. Tourne is comprised of three long tracks, each over or around the ten minute mark, and presents their take of playing live. When I’m saying that this is their take, I mean it literally. Even though there’s a certain generational gap when it comes to those two players’ age, they both refer to the early days of free improvisation (we could comment that those days where having jazz as a reference but nothing more) when a new language –every sound is possible and only the players are liable for it- was being formed and presented through playing live. This is how both of them antagonize with their preconceived ideas about playing music: by challenging each other to go further and further, even beyond the margins of what is sound, what is music, what is that should be heard from percussion and saxophones. This is not their first collaboration but, still, they sound fresh and willing not to fall in the shaky ground of presenting “good” music-not even playing “challenging” and “adventurous” stuff. They just are themselves, staying true to the basic ethos of free improvisation. Trying, at least, to present something new each time. Bennett’s playing is agile, feverish and energetic as never before. He seems to be enjoying himself as he releases low level percussive barrages. Wright, restless as ever, follows but also runs in parallel releasing saxophone sounds as if his respected instrument is made of rubber and can bend and displace notes and phrases. I’m not sure if I made my point clear out to you, but this is a joy to experience release that has to be, at least, listened by a lot of people. items.body: Label: ECM Records, 2026 Personnel - Ayumi Tanaka: piano; Thomas Morgan: bass; Thomas Strønen; drums. Japanese-born, Oslo-based pianist, composer, and improviser Ayumi Tanaka presents a new trio with in-demand American bassist Thomas Morgan and Norwegian drummer Thomas Strønen. Until now, Tanaka had released two albums— Memento (2016) and Subaqueous Silence (2019)—as a leader with her former trio, featuring Christian Meaas Svendsen on bass and Per Oddvar Johansen on drums, and she’s been a wild card in Strønen’s chamber-jazz group Time Is A Blind Guide. The new trio first played together in 2024 at Oslo’s Victoria, Nasjonal Jazzscene, and Windflower consists mostly of improvised music. The album opens with the title track, which enchants with the enveloping, organic sound that stems from continuous impressionistic pianism, sophisticated bass lyricism, and the rich embrace of percussion. It is followed by “ La Source ”, an achingly beautiful ballad wrapped in idyllic contemplation. This is the only piece written by Tanaka and reveals her maturity, intelligent restraint, and fragile melodicism. Morgan brings his hypnotic bass to the fore, while Strønen injects occasional snare fluxes, deviating attention from his light-footed toms-and-cymbals maneuvers. The piece gets intriguingly layered by the end. A gentle pulse takes over “ From Us, To You ”, enhanced by muted piano hits. A tranquil aural construction flits by expertly measured brush strokes and an elucidating, supportive bass drive. This is the kind of trio that loves to let things flow naturally and spontaneously, unattached to tempo or rigid structure. The threesome integrate their sounds as a breathing whole, and that’s noticeable on the concise “ The Sea Is Still ”, introduced by Strønen’s impeccably tuned kit and unfolding with Tanaka’s shapeless fidgeting and Morgan’s unmistakable bass foundation. It’s a shame it ends so fast. “ Spring ” is another example of graceful delicacy, while “ Driftwood ” is imbued with loose freedom yet flows with a more familiar swing vibe and pace, fusing modern classical and chamber jazz elements with refined taste. Tanaka’s concept of intent anchors the ensemble’s creative abstraction. Morgan and Strønen help her flesh out atypical yet non-discordant ideas as they share their own musical perspectives. The modern, often introspective chamber textures on Windflower bring tranquilizing comfort. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Windflower ► 02 - La Source ► 06 - The Sea Is Still

items.body:
Rachael Yamagata is returning to Singapore for a long-awaited reunion with fans. Taking place on 16 September at Foo Chow Hall, the concert marks the singer-songwriter’s first gig here since 2018, her 10th Singapore performance, and her only Southeast Asia stop for the tour.

Across more than two decades, Yamagata has built a loyal following through her unmistakable voice, cinematic songwriting, and emotionally raw performances. From her early breakthrough with Happenstance to fan favourites from Elephants…Teeth Sinking Into Heart, Chesapeake, and Tightrope Walker, her songs have travelled through albums, live rooms, TV soundtracks, and K-dramas — most notably Something in the Rain and One Spring Night. With her fifth studio album, Starlit Alchemy, Yamagata returns with a record shaped by grief, resilience, transformation, and release.

Ahead of her Singapore show, Bandwagon caught up with Yamagata to talk about her relationship with Singapore fans, the journey behind Starlit Alchemy, being discovered by a new generation through K-dramas, and what independence has taught her.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Mailive (@mailive_damai)

You’re returning to Singapore for your first show here since 2018, and it also marks your 10th Singapore performance. What comes to mind when you think about your relationship with audiences here?

Wow — 10 shows! I didn’t even realise that.

When I think of the Singapore audience, I think of beautiful moments with the audience after the shows, actually. I’ve done some really long meet-and-greet lines there in particular, and the patience of fans to stand in line for hours to say hello has really touched me. We have such a brief moment together, a hug, or quick story, but the depth and emotion from those interactions always leaves me in wonder.

Singapore has been a recurring stop for you over the years. Do you remember a particular show, fan encounter, or moment here that stayed with you?

I remember a montage of moments — being jet-lagged with the band and walking to find chicken and rice at 2 AM, soundchecking at the Esplanade when the secondary keyboard broke and we were scrambling to fix it, seeing that infinity pool on top of that one hotel and someone telling me Katy Perry made her press interviewers jump in the pool. Crazy things like that.

With the fans, I have every gift I’ve ever been given hanging in my office, so I always remember trying to fit it all in my suitcase the morning of our flight. Mostly with the audience — I remember the hugs, tears, and love exchanged.

This is your only Southeast Asia stop for the Starlit Alchemy tour. For fans travelling in from around the region, what kind of night do you hope they walk into?

I hope my show can help to move the deep emotions through the audience so they feel lighter when they leave. We are in such evolutionary times and it is a lot for our hearts and minds to process.

The songs I’ll be playing from Starlit Alchemy are made for alchemising those things weighing on your heart into something empowering, rich, and recognised. We always mix in the songs people have come to know and love, and there is a lot of laughter in the show as well. I’m hoping to do whatever I can to offer healing to the weary.

Starlit Alchemy arrived nine years after Tightrope Walker. Looking back on that time between albums, what changed in your life and your creative process?

There’s too much life to speak about in those nine years really, but when I think of those two albums side by side — Tightrope Walker is a collection of songs highlighting a search for balance, resilience, and grit really — coming into your own strength and using it to stay steady. Starlit Alchemy is falling off that tightrope and remembering you can fly.

Starlit Alchemy is described as “a map made after the journey, not before.” When did you begin to see the emotional thread connecting these songs, and how did that shape the final album?

I wrote many of the songs before 2020 and had planned to record during that year. Of course, that year changed everyone and I ended up writing more songs as my own expression of what I was experiencing through that time.

It was like weaving a tapestry without knowing what the final image would be. I initially tried recording five of the songs as one full take — they were in the same key and I would play with interludes connecting them.

As time went on and I had my own journey of highs and lows, I began to see the thread where grief and resilience meet, whether in life, love, or collective experience. The galactic aspect was born from 2020 — I went on deep dives of a cosmic reality and found a whole new world to match with my intuitive sense and questioning that has always infiltrated my writing. Somewhere in all of that, the picture began taking shape.

There’s a strong sense of transformation in this album — almost like something being shed. What did making Starlit Alchemy help you let go of?

Fear.

Happenstance introduced so many listeners to your voice and songwriting. Looking back, what do you hear now in that version of yourself?

Youth. Depth. Struggle. Defiance. The beginning.

More recently, a new generation of fans have discovered your voice through K-dramas. How did you get involved with soundtracking Ahn Pan-seok’s TV shows?

My now dear friend and sister Namyeon Lee found me. She is the brilliant composer that brought me into that world.

When you watched Something in the Rain and One Spring Night, what was it like hearing your music become part of those worlds?

I don’t really watch much I’m involved in, the same way I don’t tend to listen to albums that I’ve recorded. Mostly because I’m busy making new things. They are a moment in time for me and once they are released, my part feels complete.

It’s more interesting for me to play the songs live and have an audience energy exchange, or hear how they might’ve been affected by the song in their own lives. I think artists always have that thing where they hear what they would change when they listen to something they did again, so part of it is self-protection. I’ll go back every now and then and revisit something long after it’s out and delight a bit, but it takes time to assess it with fresh ears and eyes.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

Finally, we admire that you’ve been self-managed for over a decade now. What has independence given you that a more conventional industry path might not have?

Thank you so much, but I do have a small team now, so credit is due their way as well for sure. Mostly, I’ve gained A LOT of experience in each sector of a career. I understand much more about how pieces affect the whole and can uplift or derail the big picture.

Creatively, that’s a wonderful thing — like knowing all the characters and the challenges in a play before you write the script. The story shapes differently. On a practical level, it’s been the hardest thing and the most gratifying thing to climb these mountains. I know enough now to not feel the pressing need to justify my instincts because experience has taught me how to listen to them more. I have the scars to prove it.

I’m not sure what a more conventional path would’ve looked like for me because I think a lot still comes down to who is leading the team. Bigger resources to take more of the load off of other people and give them capacity to do stellar work, myself included — that’s the main advantage of that system I would so appreciate.

My main challenge doing so much of it myself has been burnout and necessary minutiae overtaking creative bandwidth. It’s a wonderful philosophy to think “artists just need to do the art”, but I know enough about humans, myself, and this business to know who might say such a thing and why they might be saying it.

All of my friends who are independent artists are dealing with the same challenges, just at different levels. It’s not an easy fix without revolutionising the entire industry. But I like mountains. They can be moved.

Rachael Yamagata: Starlit Alchemy Tour — Live In Singapore is presented by Bandwagon Live, in partnership with The Rock Promotions, MAILIVE, and MAISEAT. Tickets for the 16 September concert at Foo Chow Hall can be purchased here.

When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma

And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.

A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.
Berceuse
Tiny Sun will perform the entire album at Toronto�s Koerner Hall on May 14, 2026.

Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
